subject: Accounting
title: Equity Accounts
description: A quick, practical guide to Equity Accounts.

hook.text: Two founders invest $100,000 each. That $200,000 goes into equity accounts.

buildup.text: Equity accounts track owners' investments, retained earnings, and withdrawals.

discovery.text: When a business earns profit and keeps it, retained earnings grow—boosting equity.

twist.text: Dividends reduce equity. Pay out all profits and the retained earnings cushion vanishes.

climax.text: Equity is net worth—what's left after all liabilities are subtracted from assets.

punchline.text: Equity shows what the owners actually have at stake.

quiz.question: What increases retained earnings?
options: Keeping earned profits in the business

details.summary: Equity accounts represent the owners' residual claim on assets after all liabilities are settled. They include common stock, retained earnings, additional paid-in capital, and treasury stock—each telling a different part of the ownership story.
details.whyItMatters: Equity shows how much of the company truly belongs to its owners. Understanding equity accounts is essential for evaluating ownership value and understanding how profits are distributed or reinvested.
takeaways: Common stock and additional paid-in capital reflect amounts invested directly by shareholders
Retained earnings represent accumulated profits that have been reinvested rather than distributed as dividends
Treasury stock is shares the company has repurchased, reducing total equity

faq.question: What is the difference between common stock and retained earnings?
faq.answer: Common stock represents money shareholders invested by purchasing newly issued shares. Retained earnings represent profits the company earned and kept instead of paying out as dividends. Both are equity, but they originate from different sources—investment vs. operations.

faq.question: What is treasury stock?
faq.answer: Treasury stock is shares a company has repurchased from shareholders. It reduces total equity and the number of shares outstanding. Companies buy back stock to return cash to shareholders, boost earnings per share, or have shares available for employee compensation plans.
